content_html:
Mortgage interest is one of the few personal expenses you can deduct on your federal tax return, but only if you itemize. Since the standard deduction is $32,200 for married couples filing jointly in 2026, many homeowners get little or no tax benefit from their mortgage. This calculator works out your real saving by figuring your federal tax with and without the mortgage deductions, and shows how the saving changes as the loan is paid down.

How to use the calculator

  1. Mortgage amount, rate and term: the loan used to buy, build or improve your main home or a second home.
  2. Filing status and adjusted gross income: these set your tax bracket, standard deduction and some of the limits below. Adjusted gross income is the figure on Form 1040, line 11.
  3. Property taxes and state income tax: together these are your state and local tax (SALT) deduction.
  4. Charitable gifts: your other main itemized deduction.
  5. More options: points, mortgage insurance, other itemized deductions, a state tax rate if your state also allows the deduction, and older loans that keep the $1,000,000 limit.

The rules the calculator applies for 2026

  • Debt limit: interest is deductible on up to $750,000 of mortgage debt ($375,000 if married filing separately) taken out after December 15, 2017. If your average balance is higher, only a proportional share of the interest counts.
  • Points: points paid to buy your main home are generally deductible in full in the year you pay them.
  • Mortgage insurance: PMI and similar premiums are deductible again from 2026, but the deduction shrinks by 10% for each $1,000 of income above $100,000 and is gone above $109,000.
  • SALT cap: state and local taxes count up to $40,400 ($20,200 if married filing separately). The cap shrinks by 30% of income above $505,000, but not below $10,000.
  • Charity: itemizers can deduct only gifts above 0.5% of their income. People who take the standard deduction can add up to $1,000 of cash gifts ($2,000 for joint filers), so the calculator adds that to the standard deduction it compares against.
  • Top bracket: households in the 37% bracket lose 2/37 of their itemized deductions on income above that bracket's threshold.

Why the saving is often smaller than expected

A common shortcut is to multiply your mortgage interest by your tax bracket. That overstates the benefit, because the first part of your itemized deductions only replaces a standard deduction you would get anyway. Your real saving is your tax rate times the amount by which your itemized deductions exceed the standard deduction.

Worked example

With the calculator's starting figures, a married couple has a $400,000 mortgage at 6.5% over 30 years and $150,000 of adjusted gross income. They pay $6,000 of property tax and $7,000 of state income tax and give $3,000 to charity.

  • First-year mortgage interest: $25,868.36
  • Itemized deductions: $25,868.36 + $13,000 of SALT + $2,250 of charity (above the 0.5% floor) = $41,118.36
  • Alternative: the $32,200 standard deduction plus $2,000 of cash gifts = $34,200
  • Itemizing gives $6,918.36 more in deductions. At their 22% rate, the mortgage saves $1,522.04 in the first year.

The shortcut of $25,868.36 × 22% would have suggested about $5,700, nearly four times the real figure. Their effective mortgage rate after the saving is about 6.12%, and the saving falls each year as the interest portion of the payment shrinks.

Tips

  • If you are close to the standard deduction, grouping two years of charitable gifts into one year can let you itemize in alternate years.
  • Interest on a home equity loan or line of credit is deductible only when the money is used to buy, build or substantially improve the home that secures it.
  • The table assumes your income and other deductions stay the same and uses 2026 rules for every year. Brackets and the standard deduction rise with inflation, so later savings will likely be a little lower.
  • The calculator treats all income as ordinary income and leaves out the alternative minimum tax and the extra standard deduction for people 65 and older.

faq.question: Can I deduct mortgage interest if I take the standard deduction?
faq.answer: No. Mortgage interest is an itemized deduction, so it only lowers your tax if your total itemized deductions are larger than your standard deduction. Most homeowners with modest loans now take the standard deduction.

faq.question: Is interest on a second home deductible?
faq.answer: Yes, interest on a mortgage for one second home can be deducted along with your main home, as long as the combined debt stays within the $750,000 limit. Interest on a third home or an investment property is not home mortgage interest.

faq.question: Can I deduct interest on a refinanced mortgage?
faq.answer: Yes, up to the balance of the old loan that was used to buy, build or improve the home. Cash taken out for other purposes does not count, and points on a refinance are usually deducted over the life of the new loan.

faq.question: Where do I find how much mortgage interest I paid?
faq.answer: Your lender sends Form 1098 early each year showing the interest, points and mortgage insurance premiums you paid in the previous year. Use those figures on Schedule A if you itemize.

faq.question: Does the mortgage interest deduction affect my state taxes?
faq.answer: It depends on the state. Some states follow the federal itemized deductions, some have their own rules and some have no income tax. Enter your state rate under More options only if your state lets you deduct mortgage interest.
